title: Electrical power

learning_outcomes.text: recall and use P = VI, with resistance-based forms completed only after resistance is taught in Lesson 6

external_knowledge: Power is the rate of energy transfer and is measured in watts.

prior_knowledge_summary: Potential difference is energy transferred per unit charge.
Use V = W/Q and W = VQ.
Use Q = It for charge transferred by a current.
Current is charge flow through a component and potential difference is measured across it.
new_learning: Use the lesson-scoped electrical-power relationship P = VI.
not_yet_taught: resistance and its relationship with potential difference and current
e.m.f., internal resistance and network analysis

blocks.heading: Same energy, very different time
content: Two devices each transfer 600 J. One takes 10 s and the other takes 120 s. They transfer the same total energy, but do they work at the same rate?
Electrical power distinguishes how quickly energy is transferred.

figure.purpose: Create the need for a rate-of-energy-transfer quantity.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show two devices each linked to a 600 J energy bar, with clocks marked 10 s and 120 s. Leave the power comparison unanswered.
figure.alt_text: Two devices transfer the same energy in different times.

blocks.heading: Recall the general meaning of power
content: Power is the rate of energy transfer. One watt means one joule transferred each second.

From prior mechanics and Topic 1 work, P = ΔE/t. P is power in watts, W; ΔE is energy transferred in joules, J; t is time in seconds, s. The rearrangement ΔE = Pt is supporting prior knowledge, not a new Lesson 5 formula.

figure.purpose: Connect watts to joules per second and accumulated energy.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Use a one-second time strip with equal energy packets, then a unit card 1 W equals 1 J per s and the exact formula P = ΔE/t.
figure.alt_text: Energy packets transferred each second illustrate power in watts.

blocks.heading: Build P = VI from earlier ideas
content: From Lesson 4, energy transferred is ΔE = VQ. From the completed charge module, Q = It.
Substitute Q = It: ΔE = VIt. Divide by time: P = ΔE/t = VI.
Lesson formula to remember: P = VI. P is electrical power in W, V is potential difference across the component in V, and I is current through it in A.

scoped_controlled_formula.scope_note: Only P = VI is taught here. Resistance-based forms are deferred until Lesson 6.

figure.purpose: Derive P = VI using only already-taught charge and energy relationships.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Equation chain: ΔE = VQ, Q = It, ΔE = VIt, P = ΔE/t, P = VI. Use colour to track Q and t cancellation.
figure.alt_text: An equation chain derives electrical power as potential difference times current.

blocks.heading: Calculate power, then energy
content: A device has 9.0 V across it and carries 0.40 A. Its power is P = VI = 9.0 × 0.40 = 3.6 W.
If it operates for 5.0 min, first convert time: t = 300 s. Using the prior relationship ΔE = Pt gives 3.6 × 300 = 1080 J before rounding, so ΔE = 1.1 × 10^3 J, or 1.1 kJ, to 2 significant figures.
Independent check: charge transferred is Q = It = 0.40 × 300 = 120 C, and ΔE = VQ = 9.0 × 120 = 1080 J before the same final rounding.

figure.purpose: Teach the two-stage power-to-energy route with an independent earlier-lesson check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Worked layout with P = VI, minute-to-second conversion, ΔE = Pt, then a separate Q = It and ΔE = VQ check. Keep units on every line.
figure.alt_text: A worked calculation finds electrical power and energy, then checks energy through charge transfer.

blocks.heading: Why both current and potential difference matter
content: Potential difference tells us energy transferred for each coulomb. Current tells us how many coulombs pass each second. Multiplying joules per coulomb by coulombs per second gives joules per second, which is watts.
At fixed potential difference, more charge passing each second means greater power. At fixed current, more energy transferred per coulomb also means greater power.

figure.purpose: Give a unit-based causal explanation of P = VI.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show unit cancellation as J/C multiplied by C/s equals J/s. Add two small comparison panels for fixed V with larger I, and fixed I with larger V.
figure.alt_text: Unit cancellation and comparison panels explain why V times I gives power.

blocks.heading: Power is not the same as energy
content: A high-power device does not always transfer more total energy. It transfers energy faster.
A 100 W device for 2 s transfers 200 J, while a 20 W device for 30 s transfers 600 J. Always include operating time when total energy is asked for.

figure.purpose: Repair confusion between energy and power.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Compare two devices with power and time bars, calculating 200 J and 600 J visually. Label faster rate and greater total separately.
figure.alt_text: A higher-power short event transfers less total energy than a lower-power longer event.

blocks.heading: Choose the shortest valid route
content: Use P = VI when potential difference and current are known. Use P = ΔE/t when energy and time are known. Use ΔE = Pt when power and time are known.
For a mixed question, earlier relationships can supply V, I or Q before using P = VI. Carry each value with its unit and check power in watts.
Do not introduce resistance-based power forms yet. Lesson 6 first defines resistance and teaches the required relationship before deriving them.

figure.purpose: Summarise formula choice while protecting the Lesson 6 boundary.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Flow chart with data pairs V and I to P = VI; ΔE and t to P = ΔE/t; P and t to ΔE = Pt. Add a locked next-lesson box labelled resistance-based forms.
figure.alt_text: A flow chart selects power and energy equations while deferring resistance-based forms.
